content.text: I'll do it! I'll get her the best present ever.

Father ruffles your hair.
Father: That's my child. Off you go, then.

Outside the cottage door, Briarwell is waking up, and your pockets are empty. Little Bess is crying by the well in the Village Square: her rag doll is gone. East at the Old Mill, Hob the Miller keeps glancing over his shoulder before slipping behind the barn. And from the Meadow to the south comes Dunstan's jeering, and a smaller child's sobbing. Kind or cruel, any two good turns should earn enough coin for Ros's gift.
go to the meadow

The path south from the square is worn smooth by a hundred bare summer feet, and the long grass of the meadow swishes cool against your shins as you push through it. Clover and crushed mint rise up with every step, and somewhere a lark is singing its heart out overhead — the kind of morning that makes you feel like nothing bad could ever happen anywhere.

Then you hear it. A sharp, mean laugh, and underneath it, a small voice trying very hard not to cry and failing completely.

Dunstan has cornered two children near the old fence post — a boy and a girl, both younger than you, both smaller than Dunstan by a good head. He's snatched something from the boy's hand — a little carved wooden horse, by the look of it — and is holding it high above his head, grinning the grin of someone who knows exactly how tall he is. *"Jump for it,"* he says, in that lazy, horrible voice of his. *"Come on. Jump."*

He hasn't noticed you yet. The two smaller children have, though. The girl's eyes go wide and hopeful over Dunstan's shoulder, like you might be the answer to a prayer she only just thought to make.

You could call Dunstan out, try to trick him, or something else entirely — but whatever you do, the two little ones are watching, and so is the meadow, in its quiet way. The carved horse glints in the morning sun, just out of reach.
confront dunstan

You plant your feet in the grass and call out across the meadow, loud and clear. *"Oi. Dunstan."*

He turns slowly, the way he always does, like turning fast would mean he was surprised. The wooden horse is still dangling from his fist. He looks you up and down, weighing things, and then that grin comes back — a little less certain than it was, but working hard to hide it. *"What do you want?"* he says. *"Come to watch?"*

*"Give it back,"* you say. Simple as that.

Something shifts behind his eyes. He's two years older and half a head taller and he knows it, but you're standing very still and looking straight at him, and that seems to cost him something. The two little ones have gone completely quiet. The lark is still singing. A long moment stretches out between you like pulled taffy.

Then Dunstan drops the horse in the grass — not handing it over, mind you, dropping it, so it looks like his choice — and he gives you a look that says this isn't finished before he turns and slouches off toward the far end of the meadow, swatting at the tall grass with one hand.

The small boy snatches up his horse and clutches it to his chest. The girl tugs your sleeve. Between them they press a warm copper coin into your palm — apparently they came prepared for the toll. *"Thank you,"* the girl whispers, fierce and quiet, like a promise.

**One coin.** One more will buy Ros something worth giving. Little Bess is still crying by the well in the Village Square, and Hob the Miller is still sneaking behind his barn at the Old Mill — either one could be worth your while.
go to little beth and help oiut

You cut back north through the meadow, the copper coin warm in your fist, and the village square opens up around you — the old stone well at its centre, the market-day benches, a pair of neighbours gossiping by the baker's door. The smell of fresh bread drifts across the cobbles and for a moment you think of your mother, and of Ros, and of how much you want today to be perfect.

You spot Little Bess straight away. She's sitting on the well's edge with her knees pulled up and her face buried in them, her small shoulders hitching with every sob. She's younger than Ros, which means she's very young indeed, and she looks about as miserable as a person can look on a sunny morning.

You crouch down beside her. *"Bess. Hey. What's happened?"*

Her head comes up. Her face is blotchy and her eyes are red and she sniffles enormously before she can speak. *"Molly,"* she manages. *"I left her somewhere and now I can't find her and I've looked everywhere and she's GONE."* The last word wobbles dangerously back into crying.

Molly is the rag doll — you know it without asking. You've seen Bess carrying that doll around the village since before she could walk properly. Faded blue dress, yarn hair the colour of straw.

*"Where did you go this morning?"* you ask gently. *"Before you came to the square?"*

Bess scrubs her nose with her sleeve and thinks very hard. *"The meadow,"* she says. *"I was watching the butterflies."*
go to the meadow and look for the doll

Back south you go, through the square and down the worn path, the long grass parting around you just as it did before. Dunstan is nowhere to be seen now — just the lark, the clover smell, and the lazy hum of bees moving between the wildflowers. You slow your steps and start looking properly, the way your father taught you to look for kindling in the undergrowth — methodically, patch by patch, not rushing.

It takes a little while. The grass is tall enough to swallow something small without a second thought.

But then, near the old fence post where Dunstan was doing his bullying, you see a scrap of faded blue caught on a splinter of wood — and there she is. Molly the rag doll, face-down in the clover, her yarn hair spread out around her like she's sleeping. She must have tumbled from Bess's arms during all the excitement and neither of you noticed in the commotion. You pick her up and dust the grass seeds from her little dress, and she stares up at you with her two button eyes, perfectly patient.

You carry her back to the square at a trot.

The moment Bess sees what's in your hands, she lets out a sound that is half shriek and half sob and launches herself off the well's edge. She squeezes Molly so hard you half expect the button eyes to pop. Then she looks up at you, still sniffling, and presses a coin into your hand with enormous solemnity, like she's been saving it for exactly this emergency.

**Two coins.** That's enough. Old Garrick's stall waits on Market Lane to the north, and Ros's birthday is still young.

Two coins clink in your pocket as you hurry up Market Lane to Old Garrick's stall.

Old Garrick leans over his stall, eyes twinkling.
Old Garrick: A birthday, is it? Well, your coin buys any one of these.
A ribbon the colour of cornflowers.

Old Garrick: She'll wear that till it's rags.
He folds it neatly into your palm.

The sun is low and gold by the time you get home, the gift hidden behind your back.

The cottage glows with candlelight. Mother has baked a honey cake, and Ros is bouncing on her toes.
Ros: Did you get me something? Did you, did you?
Give Ros her gift.

Ros squeals and throws her arms around you.
Ros: It's perfect! You're the best!
Later, as the candles gutter, Father goes to the window and goes very still.
There is smoke rising from the woods.
Father: Charcoal burners, most likely. Off to bed, the both of you.
Go to bed.
You lie awake a long time, listening to Father's boots creak by the door.

You wake to screaming. Orange light flickers through the shutters and the air is thick with smoke. Father is at the door with his woodaxe, shouting for Mother to take Ros out the back. Then the door splinters: Red Corwin's bandits are in Briarwell. You can hide, fight, or go looking for Mother and Ros.

You throw yourself under the bed, pressing flat against the cold earthen floor, pulling the hanging blanket down to cover the gap. Dust and woodsmoke fill your nose. You clamp both hands over your mouth and breathe in tiny, careful sips.

Through the crack beneath the blanket you can see the cottage in flickering orange slices. Mother is gone. Ros is gone. The back door swings open on its leather hinge, creaking softly — they got out, they must have got out, you tell yourself, you tell yourself again.

Then the front door bursts inward with a sound like a thunderclap.

Father fills the doorway with his axe raised, a dark shape against the roaring orange outside. He looks enormous. He looks like he could stop anything. There are voices — rough, laughing voices — and a scuffle that shakes the whole cottage, and then a sound you will never forget, and then silence, and then Father is on the floor and he is not moving and the boots of two bandits are stepping over him like he is a piece of furniture.

You do not scream. You do not know how you do not scream.

The boots move through the cottage, kicking things over, and then they leave, and the orange light grows brighter, and you realise with a cold, creeping horror that the thatch above you has begun to catch.

The back door is still open. Cool night air breathes through it, and somewhere beyond it — in the square, in the dark — you can hear voices crying out. Mother and Ros are out there somewhere.

Latest assistant narrative: "You throw yourself under the bed, pressing flat against the cold earthen floor, pulling the hanging blanket down to cover the gap. Dust and woodsmoke fill your nose. You clamp both hands over your mouth and breathe in tiny, careful sips.

Through the crack beneath the blanket you can see the cottage in flickering orange slices. Mother is gone. Ros is gone. The back door swings open on its leather hinge, creaking softly — they got out, they must have got out, you tell yourself, you tell yourself again.

Then the front door bursts inward with a sound like a thunderclap.

Father fills the doorway with his axe raised, a dark shape against the roaring orange outside. He looks enormous. He looks like he could stop anything. There are voices — rough, laughing voices — and a scuffle that shakes the whole cottage, and then a sound you will never forget, and then silence, and then Father is on the floor and he is not moving and the boots of two bandits are stepping over him like he is a piece of furniture.

You do not scream. You do not know how you do not scream.

The boots move through the cottage, kicking things over, and then they leave, and the orange light grows brighter, and you realise with a cold, creeping horror that the thatch above you has begun to catch.

The back door is still open. Cool night air breathes through it, and somewhere beyond it — in the square, in the dark — you can hear voices crying out. Mother and Ros are out there somewhere."

When the shouting finally stops, the silence is worse. Grey ash drifts down over the Woods' Edge like snow.

A tall figure in a travel-stained cloak kneels beside you in the ashes.
Stranger: Easy, little one. The bandits are gone.
